podcast.title: Awful Concert Sound (1978)
podcast.body: ACDC opened for Aerosmith at the Winnipeg Arena on August 30, 1978, with Bon Scott on lead vocals. Despite the potential for an "awesome" show, the sound was described as a "blare of distortion," making the entire experience terrible. "That should have been awesome, but it wasn't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artwork Design Studio
podcast.body: Hipgnosis, a London-based design studio, created artwork for ACDC. "They did work for Pink Floyd, Led Zeppelin, ACDC, Peter Gabriel, and many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bon Scott's Tragic Death
podcast.body: Just six months after "Highway to Hell" was released, lead singer Bon Scott was found dead of alcohol poisoning at age 33 in February 1980. The band considered disbanding, as Scott was considered critical to their image. "Just six months after the release of the High Way to Hell album in February 1980, Bonscott was found dead of alcohol poisoning at age 33."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Early American Chart Struggles
podcast.body: Through 1978, none of ACDC's LPs climbed higher than number 113 on the Billboard album chart, prompting Atlantic Records executives to seek a more radio-friendly producer to elevate them from a live draw to a major US chart-topper. "Through 1978, none of ACDC's LPs got higher on the Billboard album chart than number 113."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: End of Collaboration with Mut Lang
podcast.body: After "For Those About to Rock" and "4," Mut Lang moved on from ACDC, never producing another LP for the group again. "After for those about to rock and for, Mutt Lang moved on from ACDC and Foriner."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Interactive Packaging
podcast.body: ACDC has released albums and box sets with elaborate art, including packaging that features embedded LED screens for moving pictures instead of static images. "Tool, ACDC, Pink Floyd, and others have released albums and box sets loaded with art, even to the point of including LED screens embedded in the packaging."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Live Performance Aesthetic
podcast.body: Guitarist Angus Young was known for appearing on stage in a schoolboy uniform, a distinctive part of the band's live image. "You may recall guitarist Angus Young appearing on stage in a schoolboy uniform."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Mut Lang's Guidance After Tragedy
podcast.body: After encouragement from friends and family, Mut Lang nudged ACDC to replace Bon Scott with another shrieking singer, Brian Johnson, formerly of the band Jordy, who possessed an even higher-pitched wail than Scott. "it was Mut who nudged them to replace Bonscott with another shrieking singer."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Name Origin
podcast.body: The band chose the initials ACDC, standing for alternating current and direct current, because they felt it told people they were electric. "They say they chose it because it tells people they're electric."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Operation Just Cause Playlist
podcast.body: ACDC's music was part of the playlist deployed by the US Army during Operation Just Cause in December 1989, when they bombarded the Vatican Embassy in Panama City with loud music to compel Manuel Noriega to surrender. "There was Motley Crew, there was Led Zeppelin, there was ACDC, it was actually quite the playlist."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prohibition on Sampling (Multiple Years)
podcast.body: Sampling from ACDC's music was considered extremely risky and legally problematic. The transcript warns that "woe to anyone who dared to use a sample from the Beatles or ACDC," indicating a strong stance against unauthorized use of their material. "Meanwhile, woe to anyone who dared to use a sample from the Beatles or ACDC."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Soviet Blacklist - Neo-Fascism and Violence
podcast.body: ACDC was featured on the 1985 "not recommended music" list by Soviet authorities, who cited "Neo-Fascism and Violence" as reasons for their prohibition. This strong ideological opposition positioned the group as a significant cultural threat in the eyes of the Soviet Union. "ACDC, Neo-Fascism and Violence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Soviet Blacklist Entry – Neo-Fascism and Violence
podcast.body: ACDC appeared on the Soviet Union's "not recommended music" list in 1985, categorized under the reasons of "Neo-Fascism and Violence." "ACDC, Neo-Fascism and Violence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: War on Terror Intimidation
podcast.body: During the US invasion of Iraq following 9/11 as part of the War on Terror, ACDC music was blurred from loudspeakers mounted on top of Humvees as a method to intimidate and harass Iraqi insurgents. "Kuresh were often mounted on the top of Humvees that blurred ACDC in Metallica as a way to intimidate and harass Iraqi insurgents."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
